title: A warehouse automation project's risk register: validating, rating, EMV and a trigger before peak season

objective: Developing a risk register: validating identified risks, assessing probability/impact/urgency, and classifying threats vs. opportunities
secondaryObjectives: Performing qualitative analysis: classifying risks in an RBS, applying risk matrices, and prioritizing by impact/urgency
Performing quantitative analysis: sensitivity analysis (Monte Carlo, decision trees, expected monetary value) and risk weighting
Documenting risk triggers and thresholds based on context, including causes, timing, and consequences

sources.cite: PMI, PMI Risk Management Professional (PMI-RMP) Examination Content Outline and Specifications (updated January 2023): Risk Strategy and Planning 22%, Risk Identification 23%, Risk Analysis 23%, Risk Response 13%, Monitor and Close Risks 19%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a copy of PMI's PDF hosted by a training provider. Relevant text: Risk Identification Task 3 'Document risk triggers and thresholds based on context/environment' ('Assess and document risk triggers, causes and timing'); Task 4 'Develop risk register' ('Analyze the validity of identified risks and triggers'; 'Examine the risk attributes like probability, impact, urgency'; 'Establish risk origin and ownership'; 'Classify risks as threats or opportunities'); Risk Analysis Task 1 'Perform qualitative analysis' ('Prioritize the risk based on impact, and urgency'; 'Apply the risk matrices'); Task 2 'Perform quantitative analysis' ('Perform sensitivity analysis', with Monte Carlo, decision trees, critical path and expected monetary value as examples). The objective wording is the course seed's.

The food distributor, the project, the probabilities, impacts, costs and support gauges are fictional teaching figures for exam practice, not measured values. Expected monetary value is probability times impact: 0.4 x 500 = 200 thousand dollars before the response, 0.1 x 500 = 50 after it.

brief.situation: You are the project risk manager at Harvest Lane Foods, a fictional food distributor, on a 12-week warehouse automation project: a new conveyor, picking robots and their control software, integrated with the warehouse system. Go-live is planned for week 11; the holiday peak starts in week 13. The sponsor holds a 400 thousand dollar contingency reserve.
handover: The risk management plan defines a five-by-five probability and impact matrix, says urgency breaks ties, and says responses that draw on the reserve need the sponsor.
The identification workshop was last week; its thirty lines are on your desk.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words, the contingency drawn and the docket.
Move on two weeks at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first you can read the plan or interview the vendor.
After week 12 you write the risk report and a short reflection.

plan.label: Read the risk management plan's definitions
plan.available: not busy and phase == "run" and isNull(planAt)
plan.why: Done, or finish what you are doing first.

effects.finding: Probability bands 0.1 to 0.9; impact bands by cost and days of delay; risks scoring high and due within 8 weeks are urgent; anything above 100 thousand dollars of exposure gets a quantified response for the sponsor.

vendor.label: Interview the robot vendor's project lead
vendor.available: not busy and phase == "run" and isNull(vendorAt)
vendor.why: Done, or finish what you are doing first.

effects.log: You ask how the control software is tested.

effects.finding: The software has never been tested against this warehouse system's interfaces; the vendor tests against a simulator. Two of its last three deliveries were late.

options.label: The register as validated, the ratings and EMV, the responses and the trigger that fired, the reserve drawn, and the risks closed or carried

source.note: How long each task takes and when each event arrives are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

wait.skipLabel: Go to the next risk review

source.note: How long each task takes and when each event arrives are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

then.log: Week 8: the vendor says the robot control software is six weeks late. Expediting it costs 500 thousand dollars.
Week 8: the parallel test environment catches two interface defects early; the software lands on time.
Week 10: integration test pass rate 91% against the 95% threshold.
The documented trigger fires: operations runs peak on manual picking with 20 temporary staff (60 thousand dollars); go-live moves to after peak.

else.log: Go-live goes ahead at 91%. In peak's first week the robots mis-pick 8% of orders; recovery costs 300 thousand dollars.
Week 12: the project closes its risk log for peak.

effects.log: Week 6: the sponsor asks about the robot software.
Week 8: the operations manager asks about go-live.

regPrompt.title: Week 2: the identification workshop's output
regPrompt.context: Thirty lines from the workshop, among them: 'integration may be hard', 'the robot vendor is new to us', 'the budget is tight', 'the floor slab was repaired last year', 'the conveyor is already a week late', and 'the conveyor supplier offers 4% off if we take delivery early'.

choices.label: Validate each line: rewrite real risks as cause, event and effect with an owner; move issues (the late conveyor) and assumptions (the floor) to their logs; mark the early-delivery discount as an opportunity

effects.log: The register holds 14 validated risks and one opportunity, each with an owner.

choices.feedback: A register holds validated risks with their attributes and owners, classified as threats or opportunities; issues and assumptions belong elsewhere.

choices.label: Paste all thirty lines into the register as written

effects.log: Thirty lines, several of them not risks.

choices.feedback: Vague lines, issues and constraints in a register hide the real risks.

choices.label: Keep only the five the sponsor mentioned
choices.feedback: Filtering by who spoke drops risks before they have been validated or rated.

qualPrompt.title: Week 4: rate and rank the register
qualPrompt.context: The risk management plan has a five-by-five probability and impact matrix and says urgency (how soon a risk could occur) breaks ties. Peak season starts in week 13.

choices.label: Rate each risk on the plan's matrix, add urgency, rank them, and group them by the risk breakdown structure

effects.log: Top of the list: R2 software delivery (probability 0.4, high impact, urgent) and R5 go-live before peak.

choices.feedback: Qualitative analysis applies the plan's matrix and prioritizes by impact and urgency.

choices.label: Rate everything medium so the sponsor is not alarmed
choices.feedback: A flat rating hides the risks that need responses first.

choices.label: Rank them by feel; the matrix takes too long
choices.feedback: Without the plan's definitions, ratings cannot be compared or defended.

emvPrompt.title: Week 6: what to do about R2
emvPrompt.context: R2: probability 0.4 that the robot control software is late, costing about 500 thousand dollars to expedite. A parallel test environment (80 thousand) would let the vendor test against the real interfaces and cut the probability to about 0.1. The vendor also offers a guaranteed-delivery addendum for 220 thousand dollars.

choices.label: Work out the expected monetary value (0.4 x 500 = 200 before, 0.1 x 500 = 50 after) and recommend the 80 thousand dollar mitigation to the sponsor: it buys 150 thousand of expected value

effects.log: The sponsor approves the mitigation from the contingency reserve.

choices.feedback: Quantitative analysis such as EMV compares a response's cost with the exposure it removes.

choices.label: Accept it: the vendor says it will be fine

effects.log: R2 accepted, with no reserve set aside.

choices.feedback: Accepting a high, urgent risk without analysis or a reserve leaves the exposure in place.

choices.label: Buy the vendor's guaranteed-delivery addendum for 220 thousand dollars
choices.feedback: Transfer works, but it costs more than the exposure it removes (EMV 200).

trigPrompt.title: Week 8: go-live is the week before peak
trigPrompt.context: Go-live is planned for week 11; peak season starts in week 13. The operations manager asks what happens if integration testing is not ready.

choices.label: Document R5's trigger and threshold: if the integration test pass rate is below 95% by week 10, run peak on manual picking with temporary staff (60 thousand dollars) and go live after peak; owner, the operations manager

effects.log: Trigger, threshold, response and owner recorded.

choices.feedback: A trigger states the observable condition, its timing and the threshold that starts the response.

choices.label: Note 'keep an eye on testing' in the register
choices.feedback: 'Keep an eye on it' names no condition, threshold or owner, so nothing starts the response.

choices.label: No need: the vendor's test plan covers it
choices.feedback: The vendor's plan is not the project's response to its own go-live risk.

reflection.question: Write the risk report for the sponsor: how the register was built and rated, how R2 was analyzed and treated, and what R5's trigger did.

parts.label: Register and ratings
parts.criteria: Validates the lines into risks with cause, event and effect and owners; separates issues and assumptions; classifies the opportunity; rates on the plan's matrix with urgency.
parts.modelAnswer: Of thirty lines, 14 were risks, rewritten with cause, event and effect and owners; the late conveyor went to the issue log and the floor to the assumption log; the discount is an opportunity. On the plan's matrix with urgency, R2 and R5 ranked first.

parts.label: Analysis, response and trigger
parts.criteria: Calculates R2's EMV before and after the response and compares it with the cost; documents R5's trigger, threshold, response and owner, and says it fired.
parts.modelAnswer: R2's EMV was 200 thousand dollars; an 80 thousand test environment brought it to 50, and the software landed on time. R5's trigger was a pass rate below 95% by week 10; it fired at 91%, so peak ran on manual picking and go-live followed.

materialized.body: A documented trigger with a threshold and an owner would have started the fallback at 91%.

overspend.body: R2 was accepted without analysis; its 500 thousand dollar impact exceeded the whole reserve.

scoring.modelReasoning: A register holds validated risks: each a cause, an uncertain event and an effect, with probability, impact, urgency and an owner; issues and assumptions go to their own logs and opportunities are classified as such. Qualitative analysis applies the plan's matrix and urgency so the urgent, high risks rise. For a risk with large exposure, expected monetary value (probability times impact) compares the response's cost with the exposure it removes: 200 down to 50 for 80 is worth it; 220 for a 200 exposure is not. A trigger is an observable condition with a threshold and timing that starts a documented response: below 95% by week 10, run peak on manual picking.
